idiom_name: stateless class behind an interface, registered in Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection
implementation_notes: Write the operation as a stateless class - no mutable fields, collaborators as readonly properties or primary-constructor parameters (C# 12) - and let the container own its lifetime: services.AddScoped<IFundsTransfer, FundsTransferService>(). The hand-wired factory or singleton that older DDD texts describe is replaced by the container's registration and lifetime management, and the class stays a plain POCO in the domain project, with domain-facing abstractions such as IInvoiceNumberGenerator implemented by infrastructure. A static class of pure functions is the lighter alternative when the operation has no collaborators; keep the injected class when the operation needs a repository or a policy to be substituted in tests.
pitfalls: A singleton registration is safe only while the service is truly stateless; the moment it takes a scoped dependency (DbContext, unit of work) the lifetime must become scoped or the container will fault.
Framework attributes on the domain class (ORM annotations, MVC filters) leak the framework into the domain layer; keep the class plain and do the registration in the composition root.
Constructor-injected mutable state (a cached rate table, a mutable collection) is shared by every caller of the same instance - the equivalent of a global variable with better manners.
